deep.reconstruction:
Context: Chapter 7 of the 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina' (E792). For a divisor d, Euler writes μ for the number of residues below d that are prime to d (μ = φ(d)). For each such b he lists the powers b^k mod d until the residue 1 returns. The least such exponent n is the multiplicative order ord_d(b). He then compares n with μ.

(a) End of §235, d = 11, μ = 10. The tables continue from the previous page.
- b=4: 1,4,5,9,3,1, so ord_11(4) = 5.
- b=5: 1,5,3,4,9,1, so ord = 5.
- b=6: 1,6,3,7,9,10,5,8,4,2,1, so ord = 10.
- b=7: 1,7,5,2,3,10,4,6,9,8,1, so ord = 10.
- b=8: 1,8,9,6,4,10,3,2,5,7,1, so ord = 10.
- b=9: 1,9,4,3,5,1, so ord = 5.
- b=10: 1,10,1, so ord = 2.
Together with the previous page (b=1: 1, b=2: 10, b=3: 5), the orders 1,10,5,5,5,10,10,10,5,2 all divide 10. The four elements of order 10 (2,6,7,8) are the primitive roots mod 11.

(b) §236, d = 12, μ = φ(12) = 4. The units are b = 1,5,7,11. We have 5^2 = 25 ≡ 1, 7^2 = 49 ≡ 1 and 11^2 = 121 ≡ 1 (mod 12). So n = 1,2,2,2. Euler remarks that always n < μ: n = μ/2 in three cases and n = μ/4 once. Thus there is no primitive root mod 12; the group is (Z/2)^2.

(c) §237, d = 13, μ = 12. Euler gives ord_13(b) for b = 1..12 without tables: 1,12,3,6,4,12,12,4,3,6,12,2.

(d) §238. For every d, ord(1) = 1. Also (d−1)^2 = d^2 − 2d + 1 ≡ 1 (mod d), while d−1 ≢ 1. Hence ord(d−1) = 2. The tacit hypothesis d > 2 is mine. For the other b, Euler says judgement is harder.

(e) §239. Suppose bc = kd + 1, i.e. bc ≡ 1 (mod d), and b^n ≡ 1. Then (bc)^n ≡ 1. Also b^n c^n ≡ c^n. Hence c^n ≡ 1. In modern terms: if b^n ≡ 1 then (b^{-1})^n ≡ 1.

(f) §240, completed on the next page. If n is the least exponent with b^n ≡ 1 and bc ≡ 1, then the least exponent for c is n or a smaller exponent. Symmetry of the argument shows it is exactly n. So ord(b^{-1}) = ord(b). The step that the order of c is an aliquot part of n is stated here and justified elsewhere (order divides any exponent giving 1).
errors: No computational errors: every residue table for d=11 and d=12 and every order listed for d=13 checks out.
§238 tacitly assumes d > 2. For d = 2 we have d−1 = 1, which has n = 1, and the claim that the first power is never ≡ 1 fails. This is trivial.
§240: the claim that the smaller exponent must be an aliquot part of n is used here without proof on this page. It follows from the standard fact that the order divides any exponent m with b^m ≡ 1.

results.what: Tables of powers and multiplicative orders mod 11, 12, 13; observed that orders divide φ(d), and that some residues have order φ(d) (mod 11, 13) while none do mod 12
results.modern_name: Multiplicative order; Euler–Fermat theorem; existence/non-existence of primitive roots
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (little theorem), Euler (generalization 1760s, primitive roots 1773/74), Gauss (proof of primitive roots for primes, Disquisitiones 1801)

results.what: If bc ≡ 1 (mod d), then b and c have the same multiplicative order
results.modern_name: Order of an element equals order of its inverse
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa residua, E262, and this Tractatus)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the published Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (Opera Postuma 1862), c. 1750s. The page is routine tables of multiplicative orders plus the elementary inverse-order lemma, all well known as Euler's.

checkable.sympy: all(n_order(mod_inverse(b, 13), 13) == n_order(b, 13) for b in range(1, 13))
checkable.asserts: §239–240: inverse has same order (e.g. 5 and 8 both order 4)
